tool.name: LongestLineFetch

summary.para: Finds the longest straight line that fits entirely inside each polygon -- the fetch when the polygon is a body of water: the longest straight path over which wind can raise waves. Holes block the line; the line passes through two polygon vertices and may extend past them to the boundary; every feature reports its line with endpoints, geodesic length and azimuth. A second mode casts directional fetch rays from station points at a fixed bearing increment, each ending at the first shoreline or an optional maximum fetch distance, with a per-station summary. A modernized, vectorized port of Jeff Jenness's classic ArcView Longest Straight Line extension -- what once ran overnight now runs in seconds. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
Finds the longest straight line that fits entirely inside each polygon. On a lake or bay this is the fetch -- the longest open-water path wind can blow along, the quantity behind wave-height and shoreline-exposure models. This is not the distance between the two farthest boundary points (that line usually leaves the polygon); it is the longest line that never crosses the boundary, and interior holes (islands) block it.
How it works. The classic result from the original ArcView extension still drives the search: the optimal line must pass through two polygon vertices, though it may extend past them until it meets the boundary (picture a line pivoting through a doorway -- it settles against two corners). The original tool clipped a line for every vertex pair and warned that it "requires a polygon theme, and lots of time"; this version replaces that with a two-phase vectorized search -- the longest uncrossed vertex-to-vertex chord is found first with batched geometry (establishing a strong lower bound), then only candidates whose upper bound (the convex-hull chord along their line) could still win are examined exactly, in descending order, stopping the moment no remaining candidate can beat the best. The result is exact, and polygons that once took hours finish in seconds.
Longest-line outputs: one line per polygon with Src_FID, Part (which part of a multipart feature holds it), Length_m (geodesic meters), Azimuth (degrees clockwise from north), the endpoint coordinates X1/Y1/X2/Y2, and any transferred attribute fields (reserved names arrive under a Src_ prefix, as in the Centerline and Width tool).
Directional fetch from stations. The second mode casts rays from each station point every N degrees, terminating each at the first shoreline crossing or at an optional maximum fetch distance (beyond which sea conditions are effectively fully developed and more open water no longer matters). Alongside the sampled rays, every station also gets two exact answers: the longest single ray from the station (MaxRay) and the longest straight line through the station (MaxChord) -- exact because the optimal line through a fixed point must touch a polygon vertex (the same convexity argument behind the two-vertex theorem), so only the directions toward each vertex need testing. The rays output carries a Kind field (Ray / MaxRay / MaxChord); the per-station summary reports the ray statistics (mean / min / max / SD and the bearing of the longest sampled ray) plus MaxRay_m / MaxRay_Brg and MaxChrd_m / MaxChrdBrg for the exact lines. Stations that fall on land are nudged to the nearest point inside the water, with the move recorded in Shift_Dist and Shift_Brg -- the behavior of this mode's ancestor, the author's UOGML Wave Energy extension (Jenness 2014, University of Guam Marine Laboratory), which implemented the wave-height and wave-energy formulas of Ekebom et al. (2003, Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science 57:887-898) on exactly these fetch rays.
Geographic data. Polygons in latitude/longitude are solved in a feature-centered azimuthal-equidistant working projection and the final line's length is reported geodesically. In directional mode every station gets its own azimuthal-equidistant projection, so radial distances from the station are true geodesic distances and bearings are true azimuths. Very large polygons (spanning more than about 1,000 km) draw a warning: at that scale a planar solve can err by a fraction of a percent, and a true spherical great-circle mode is a planned addition.
Geometry notes. Layer selections are honored; multipart features report the best line over their parts; true-curve boundaries (geodatabase circles and arcs) are densified automatically, so on curved boundaries the answer is exact to the densification resolution (about 1/500 of the outline length).
Why the simplify tolerance matters. The candidate search grows with the square of the vertex count, so boundary detail is the entire cost of this tool -- and much of that detail is often meaningless. A corridor or lake traced from a raster carries a stair-step boundary with a vertex at every cell corner: tens of thousands of vertices that describe the cell size, not the shape. The Advanced simplify tolerance generalizes each boundary before the search (both modes), collapsing those steps; a tolerance near the raster's cell size typically cuts vertex counts -- and run times -- by an order of magnitude or more, while moving the boundary (and therefore the answer) by no more than about the tolerance. A 22-minute raster-traced corridor can finish in seconds at a cell-size tolerance, with the fetch length changed by only a few meters. Concretely, a 20-meter tolerance says the simplified boundary may stray up to about 20 m from the digitized one: shoreline features shallower than ~20 m are flattened away, larger ones survive, and the computed lines can shift by up to roughly that distance -- so choose the smallest shoreline feature that should still matter. Leave it blank to honor the exact boundary as digitized -- appropriate for hand-digitized shorelines whose vertices are all real. Be prepared for LONG runs on detailed boundaries (a single detailed lake can present tens of millions of candidate vertex pairs), and watch the progress bar: it names the polygon being worked, the search stage ("screening vertex pair..." then "verifying candidate line...") and the count completed of the total, so you always know what the tool is doing and can decide early whether to cancel and set a tolerance instead. The run messages also report each large polygon's vertex and candidate-pair counts, so it is easy to see when simplification would help. The tolerance matters far LESS in directional mode: rays are cast against the boundary's edges directly, so that cost grows with rays times boundary detail, not with the square of the vertex count.
Relation to Esri's tools. ArcGIS Pro has no tool for the longest interior line: Minimum Bounding Geometry fits shapes around a polygon and ignores containment, and Polygon Main Angle reports only an orientation. This tool fills that gap at every license level, in both modes.

dialogReference.para: Longest line in each polygon: one line per polygon -- the fetch.

Directional fetch rays from station points: rays every N degrees from each station, ending at the first shoreline or the maximum fetch distance. The output also includes, for every station, the exact longest ray and the exact longest line through the station -- these generally do not fall on one of the ray increments (the Kind field tells them apart).

param.name: in_features
param.displayname: Polygons (the water bodies or similar analysis boundaries)

dialogReference.para: The polygons whose longest interior line is wanted -- most often water bodies (lakes, bays, reservoirs), but any analysis boundary works the same way: habitat patches, corridors, management units, burn perimeters. Interior holes (islands) block the line.
The points to cast fetch rays from. Stations that fall on land are nudged to the nearest point inside the water, with the move recorded in Shift_Dist / Shift_Brg.

param.name: transfer_fields
param.displayname: Attribute fields to transfer (from the polygons, or from the stations in directional mode)

dialogReference.para: Fields whose values ride along onto every output feature, next to the automatic Src_FID. Reserved or conflicting names arrive under a Src_ prefix with the source values intact.

param.name: bearing_increment
param.displayname: Bearing increment between rays (degrees; directional mode)

dialogReference.para: The angle between successive fetch rays -- 10 degrees casts 36 rays per station; 5 degrees casts 72.

param.name: max_fetch
param.displayname: Maximum fetch distance (optional; rays stop here even over open water)

dialogReference.para: Rays stop at this distance even without meeting a shoreline (the Capped field marks them). In wave modeling, fetch beyond some distance no longer increases wave height -- the sea is fully developed. Also keeps open-ocean stations from casting effectively infinite rays.

param.name: linear_units
param.displayname: Units for the maximum fetch distance

dialogReference.para: Meters, Kilometers, Feet or Miles for the maximum fetch distance. Output length fields are always in meters.
One line per polygon: Src_FID, Part, Length_m (geodesic), Azimuth (degrees clockwise from north), X1/Y1/X2/Y2 endpoint coordinates, plus transferred fields.

Every ray from every station, plus two exact lines per station: Kind (Ray / MaxRay / MaxChord), Src_FID (the station), Bearing, Fetch_m (meters), and Capped (1 when the line stopped at the maximum fetch distance rather than a shoreline), plus transferred fields. MaxRay is the exact longest single ray; MaxChord is the exact longest straight line through the station.

param.name: simplify_tolerance
param.displayname: Simplify tolerance (boundaries simplified before the analysis; blank = use the exact boundary)

dialogReference.para: Advanced: generalize each boundary by this distance before the analysis (both modes). The longest-line search grows with the square of the vertex count, and raster-traced boundaries carry a vertex at every cell corner -- detail that describes the cell size, not the shape. A tolerance near the raster cell size collapses the stair-steps, typically cutting run times from minutes to seconds, while the answer shifts by no more than about the tolerance.

What a value means, concretely: entering 20 meters says the simplified boundary may stray up to about 20 m from the digitized one. Every cove, notch or stair-step shallower than ~20 m is flattened away (and its vertices dropped); every feature larger than that survives. The computed lines can therefore shift by up to roughly 20 m -- a ray may end ~20 m earlier or later where the shoreline moved -- so set the tolerance to the size of the smallest shoreline feature that should still matter to the analysis.

Leave blank for the exact boundary as digitized -- right for hand-digitized shorelines whose vertices are all real. The tolerance is in the unit chosen in the Units for the distances dropdown (Meters by default) -- not the polygon's coordinate-system units; the tool converts internally, including for latitude/longitude data.

param.name: out_stations
param.displayname: Output station summary points (optional; directional mode)

dialogReference.para: One point per station (at its used, possibly nudged, location): FetchMean / FetchMin / FetchMax / FetchSD over the sampled rays, MaxF_Brg (bearing of the longest sampled ray), the exact MaxRay_m / MaxRay_Brg and MaxChrd_m / MaxChrdBrg lines, and Shift_Dist / Shift_Brg recording any on-land nudge. All lengths in meters.

scriptExample.title: Longest Line in Polygon (Fetch) example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The fetch line of every lake, then directional fetch rays every 10 degrees from monitoring stations.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # mode options (matching is by prefix): # "Longest line in each polygon (the fetch)" # "Directional fetch rays from station points" # linear_units: "Meters" / "Kilometers" / "Feet" / "Miles" arcpy.jenness.LongestLineFetch( mode="Longest line in each polygon (the fetch)", in_features=r"D:\data\lakes.gdb\lakes", transfer_fields="Lake_Name", out_lines=r"D:\data\lakes.gdb\lake_fetch_lines") arcpy.jenness.LongestLineFetch( mode="Directional fetch rays from station points", in_features=r"D:\data\lakes.gdb\lakes", stations=r"D:\data\lakes.gdb\wave_stations", bearing_increment=10.0, max_fetch=50.0, linear_units="Kilometers", out_radials=r"D:\data\lakes.gdb\station_fetch_rays", out_stations=r"D:\data\lakes.gdb\station_fetch_summary")
